title: How to Develop Software Engineering Skills in the Age of AI
gist: Chelsea Troy argues that AI tools speed up outcomes but not skill building, which still needs slow, effortful learning (spaced repetition, predicting outcomes, varied formats). Pressure for ever-faster output pushes developers into shortcuts they never revisit, a systemic risk to the junior talent pipeline that managers need to guard against.

insights.claim: Software engineering has two modes, figuring things out and doing things, and when doing depends on figuring out, trying to go faster leaves engineers stuck.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: AI productivity gains may stall on novel problems that require understanding, so headline speedup claims overstate the effect.
insights.quote: we have to downshift to get anywhere
insights.locator: There are two modes of software engineering

insights.claim: Using tools including AI as outcome accelerants often does not support skill development, since engineers still need to understand how the systems they modify work.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Heavy AI-assisted coding may erode deep system knowledge in engineering organizations, a hidden long-term cost.
insights.quote: Even with AI available to us, we need to understand how the systems we are trying to modify work

insights.claim: Learning activities are inefficient by design because the discomfort of confusion and frustration is what builds cognitive capacity.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Removing friction with AI may remove the mechanism by which engineers become senior.
insights.quote: It is that uncomfortable emotion, the confusion, the frustration, that is necessary for us to build cognitive capacity.

insights.claim: Generative AI has changed the software skills landscape, but the biology and psychology of human problem-solving has not changed, so understanding how people learn matters more than understanding the tools.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Human learning limits stay the binding constraint on engineering capability even as tools improve.
insights.locator: Generative AI has changed the landscape

themes.theme: Systemic pressure and the junior pipeline

insights.claim: Expectations of ever-increasing work pace raise the stakes of learning barriers, forcing developers into shortcuts they never revisit, a systemic problem managers must address by managing upwards.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: AI-driven productivity targets risk hollowing out skill formation, creating future talent shortages and quality risk.
insights.quote: developers feel forced to take shortcuts, and they never come back for the learning objective
insights.locator: InfoQ: What are the cognitive barriers

insights.claim: Learners increasingly conflate work completed with learning objective accomplished; having Claude write a teaching-exercise compiler misses the point, since the compiler was a toy problem for learning to think.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Education and junior training models must change as AI makes artifact production trivial.
insights.quote: Sure, Claude can write the compiler, but that completely misses the point, because the point was never the compiler.
insights.locator: InfoQ: How can we enable learning

insights.claim: The key performance indicator for learning is the change in the practitioner's thinking, not the quality of the produced artifact, and seniors must closely observe juniors' actual work to coach that change.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Output-based productivity metrics misjudge junior development in AI-assisted teams.

insights.claim: Skill development at its core requires focused attention interspersed with quality sleep, so seniors should spread a junior's learning across several sleep cycles (spaced repetition).
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Effective upskilling takes calendar time that AI cannot compress.

insights.claim: Outcome prediction, stopping at each step to guess what comes next and why before checking, greatly increases how well learners internalize information.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Suggests a way to design AI coding tools that support learning rather than replace it.

insights.claim: People learn better from the same information in several formats, and self-described kinesthetic learners are really benefiting from meeting the material a second or third time when they try it.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Supports multi-format training products over single-mode learning-style approaches.
insights.quote: It is the second or sometimes the third way in which they are encountering this information; that's when it sticks.
